bean-common-mosaic-virus.summary: Bean common mosaic virus infects beans and several other legumes. Affected leaves may show an uneven light-and-dark green pattern, puckering or curling, and plants infected early can remain small. The virus travels in infected seed and can be carried between plants by aphids during short feeding visits. Symptoms vary with the plant variety and virus strain, and some infections are easily confused with other bean viruses. Starting with tested seed is therefore more reliable than judging seed health by its appearance.

sources.label: UC IPM: Bean Common Mosaic
Jordan and Hammond 2020: BCMV and BCMNV

batrachochytrium-dendrobatidis.summary: Bd chytrid fungus is a microscopic fungus that infects amphibian skin. It releases swimming spores into water, allowing infection to pass through wet environments. Some amphibians carry it without obvious illness, while others develop chytridiomycosis, with abnormal skin shedding, weakness or loss of normal movement. Severe outbreaks have contributed to amphibian declines around the world. A skin swab can reveal infection, but visible illness is not specific enough to identify the fungus, and detecting it does not always mean the animal has developed disease.

sources.label: Cornell Wildlife Health Lab: Chytridiomycosis
USGS: Amphibian disease research

casuarina-equisetifolia.summary: Beach sheoak is a tall flowering tree whose fine, drooping branchlets can make it look like a pine. Its true leaves are tiny scales arranged in rings around those jointed branchlets, and the fruits form small woody, cone-like clusters. Native across parts of Asia and the western Pacific, it has been planted widely in tropical regions. In Florida, it is one of several introduced Casuarina species that have spread into native plant communities. Counting the leaf scales helps distinguish it from related sheoaks.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: Field Guide to Common Casuarina Species in Florida
Kew POWO: Casuarina equisetifolia, general information

crepis-vesicaria.summary: Beaked hawksbeard is a leafy herb with yellow, dandelion-like flower heads and toothed or lobed leaves. The outer rays can be reddish underneath, a useful detail when similar yellow-flowered plants grow together. Mature seeds narrow into a slender beak before the tuft of hairs used for wind dispersal. Native to parts of Europe, the Mediterranean and nearby Atlantic islands, it has been introduced elsewhere. North American records include disturbed places, meadows and fields, although its local abundance varies considerably.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust: Crepis vesicaria
Kew POWO: Crepis vesicaria

aphis-fabae.summary: Bean aphids are small, dark sap-feeding insects that gather on tender growth, leaves and stems. Adults are usually dull dark green to purplish black with lighter legs; both winged and wingless forms occur. Dense colonies can curl foliage and weaken young bean plants, while their sugary honeydew leaves surfaces sticky and encourages sooty mold. They can also carry plant viruses. Lady beetles, lacewings and tiny parasitic wasps often reduce colonies naturally, so the presence of aphids does not always mean treatment is needed.

sources.label: NCSU: Pests of Beans and Peas
UC IPM: Aphids on dry beans

megalurothrips-usitatus.summary: Bean flower thrips is a small insect most often found inside legume flowers. Adults are dark brown, with pale areas on the narrow wings, while males can be smaller and lighter. Feeding and egg laying can damage flowers and developing pods, reducing crop quality. The species is associated with tropical Asia and has more recently been recorded in Florida. Several thrips can share the same bean crop, so an insect in a damaged blossom needs microscopic examination before it can be confidently named.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: Bean Flower Thrips
Thysanoptera Californica: Megalurothrips usitatus

smynthurodes-betae.summary: Bean root aphids are small, pale insects that feed on the roots of beans and many other plants. The wingless root-feeding forms are yellowish white with a dusting of wax and a light brown head and legs. Their life cycle can also involve Pistacia trees, where colonies develop inside swellings formed from leaf tissue. In places without those tree hosts, populations may remain on roots. This broad choice of hosts means the name describes only part of the aphid's way of life.

sources.label: Smynthurodes betae — Aphids on the World’s Plants
Smynthurodes betae — AphID
Gall defense and facilitation in Smynthurodes betae

acanthoscelides-obtectus.summary: Bean weevil is a small seed beetle that develops inside dry beans. Adults have mottled brown, black and gray wing covers and lack the long snout associated with true weevils. The larvae chew within seeds, often remaining hidden until an adult leaves a neat round exit hole. Infestations can begin in the field and continue through repeated generations in warm storage. Moving infested seed has carried the beetle widely, and apparently intact beans can already contain developing larvae.

sources.label: Rutgers: Bean Weevil
Canadian Grain Commission: Bean weevil

acanthus-mollis.summary: Bear’s breeches is a clump-forming perennial with large, glossy leaves cut into deep lobes. Tall flower spikes rise above the foliage, carrying white flowers surrounded by purple-toned, spiny structures. The leaf shape is familiar from classical architectural decoration. Native around parts of the Mediterranean, it is grown widely as an ornamental in sun or partial shade. Underground stems allow an established clump to spread, and pieces left in the soil can make it difficult to remove completely.

sources.label: NCSU: Acanthus mollis
Kew POWO: Acanthus mollis

polypogon-viridis.summary: Beardless rabbitsfoot grass is a moisture-loving grass that forms loose tufts and can spread through creeping stems that root where they touch the ground. Its narrow, flat leaves rise beneath dense, branched flower heads, usually green and sometimes tinged purple. Unlike the conspicuously bristly heads of some related grasses, its tiny flower clusters lack long awns. It grows beside ditches and waterways and on other damp ground, with a native range spanning parts of southern Europe, Africa and Asia.

sources.label: Go Botany: Polypogon viridis
Flora of New Zealand: Polypogon viridis

cimex-lectularius.summary: Bed bugs are small, blood-feeding insects that hide in narrow spaces close to where people rest. Unfed adults are flat, oval and brown, roughly the size of an apple seed; after feeding they become fuller and redder. Young bugs are smaller and much paler. They shelter in mattress seams, bed frames, furniture and other cracks, and can travel with luggage or belongings. Finding the insect itself, shed skins or dark spotting is more useful for identification than a pattern of skin bites.

sources.label: Bed Bugs Appearance and Life Cycle
Bed bugs

phyllaphis-fagi.summary: Beech aphids are tiny sap-feeding insects most easily noticed through the white, woolly wax that gathers beneath beech leaves. The insects underneath are pale yellow, and their feeding can curl leaves downward. Sticky honeydew may fall onto lower foliage and support dark sooty mold. On European beech, eggs spend winter in bark crevices before colonies develop on new leaves. Infestations can spoil the appearance of leaves, although established, healthy trees often tolerate them without lasting harm.

sources.label: Woolly beech aphid
Study on intensity of infestation, biology and harmfulness of woolly beech aphid

neonectria-coccinea.summary: Neonectria coccinea is a fungus associated with bark disease in European beech. It can live in beech tissues without obvious symptoms, but it has also been recovered from declining trees and shown experimentally to cause substantial bark lesions. These injured patches can be part of more complicated tree decline involving stress and other fungi. The species is closely related to fungi involved in North American beech bark disease, so an affected tree's appearance alone cannot establish which fungus is present.

sources.label: Phylogenetic relationships of Neonectria/Cylindrocarpon on Fagus in North America
Fungi Associated With Woody Tissues of European Beech and Their Impact on Tree Health

neonectria-faginata.summary: Neonectria faginata is one of the fungi involved in beech bark disease in North America. The disease develops through an interaction between beech scale insects and fungi: scale feeding damages the bark, creating entry points for infection. Affected American beeches develop sunken or swollen areas of dead bark that may merge into larger cankers. The white, woolly material often seen earlier on the trunk belongs to the scale insects. Fungal identification requires closer examination than the tree's outward symptoms.

sources.label: Phylogenetic relationships of Neonectria/Cylindrocarpon on Fagus in North America
Beech bark disease

beech-leaf-disease.summary: Beech leaf disease is associated with a microscopic leaf nematode, Litylenchus crenatae subsp. mccannii. A distinctive early sign is dark banding between the veins of beech leaves, especially when viewed against the light. More affected leaves may become thick, curled or misshapen, while damaged buds produce fewer leaves and the crown gradually thins. The nematodes spend winter in buds and affect developing foliage. American, European and Oriental beeches can develop the disease, so host species alone does not rule it out.

sources.label: Beech Leaf Disease in Maryland
Beech leaf disease symptoms caused by newly recognized nematode subspecies Litylenchus crenatae mccannii

litylenchus-crenatae-ssp-mccannii.summary: The beech tree nematode is a microscopic roundworm associated with beech leaf disease. It lives in developing buds and leaves, where its presence is linked to dark bands between leaf veins and to thickened, distorted foliage. Heavy damage can prevent buds from opening normally and leave the crown sparse. Researchers distinguished this North American subspecies from the previously described Japanese Litylenchus crenatae using body features and DNA, and reproduced disease symptoms by introducing nematodes into beech buds.

sources.label: Beech Leaf Disease in Maryland
Beech leaf disease symptoms caused by newly recognized nematode subspecies Litylenchus crenatae mccannii

perilla-frutescens.summary: Beefsteakplant is an aromatic annual in the mint family, native to Asia and introduced in many parts of North America. It has opposite, toothed leaves on square stems, with small flowers grouped along upright spikes. Common ornamental forms have broad, crinkled, purple to reddish leaves. Plants produce abundant seed and may appear beyond gardens along roadsides or in other disturbed ground. Despite its history of cultivation, it can be troublesome in pastures because the plant is toxic to livestock.

sources.label: Perilla frutescens
Perilla frutescens — Plants of the World Online

spodoptera-exigua.summary: Beet armyworm is a moth whose caterpillars feed on many vegetables, field crops and weeds. Young larvae gather together and scrape leaf surfaces, sometimes leaving thin, windowlike patches and loose webbing. Older caterpillars spread out, chew irregular holes and may enter developing fruit. They are usually green with lengthwise stripes and a small dark spot near the second pair of true legs. Adults are mottled gray-brown moths, while eggs occur in clusters beneath a covering of pale, hairlike scales.

sources.label: Beet armyworm, Spodoptera exigua
Beet Armyworm — Peppers

lonicera-x-bella.summary: Bell's honeysuckle is a dense, many-stemmed shrub produced by crosses between Morrow's and Tatarian honeysuckles. It bears opposite, oval leaves and paired tubular flowers, often pink when fresh and yellow as they age. Red or orange berries follow and can be carried by birds. The hybrid is variable, with leaves and twigs ranging from nearly hairless to lightly downy. In parts of the northeastern and midwestern United States it grows along woodland edges, roadsides and old fields, sometimes forming dense stands.

sources.label: Bell’s honeysuckle — Wisconsin DNR
Flora Novae Angliae: Lonicera morrowii × L. tatarica hybrid paragraph

polygonum-patulum.summary: Polygonum patulum is a slender annual knotweed with upright stems that branch near the base. Narrow, pointed leaves are larger low on the plant and become much smaller toward the flowering branches. Tiny greenish or pink flowers gather around the stem joints, with many crowded near branch tips. Thin, papery sheaths surround the joints below the leaves. Native across parts of Europe and Asia, it occurs in fields, gardens and other open ground, including seasonally flooded places.

sources.label: Polygonum patulum — Flora of Iraq account and Kew range
Polygonum — Flora of China key

jatropha-gossypiifolia.summary: Bellyache bush is a branching tropical shrub with leaves divided into three to five pointed lobes. Leaf stalks and margins carry sticky, gland-tipped hairs, and the foliage may be green or reddish purple. Small red to purple flowers develop in clusters, followed by rounded seed capsules. Native from Mexico through tropical America, it has escaped cultivation elsewhere. In northern Australia it forms dense stands around waterways and disturbed land. Its toxicity makes it a concern where people or livestock might consume it.

sources.label: Bellyache bush — Northern Territory Government
Jatropha gossypiifolia — Flora of the Cayman Islands and Kew

ptinus-bicinctus.summary: Belted spider beetles are small beetles that sometimes occur in stored products and buildings. Adults are roughly two to four millimeters long, with patches of pale scales near the front and rear of their wing covers. Males are more parallel-sided, while females look rounder. The species is native to Europe and North Africa and has been introduced to North America. Canadian records include warehouses and homes, and an early United States report documented it breeding in bags of stored flour.

sources.label: Beetles associated with stored products in Canada: an identification guide
Annotated list of insects and mites associated with stored grain and cereal products

thunbergia-grandiflora.summary: Bengal trumpet is a long-lived climbing vine with large, pale blue to violet flowers and pale throats. Its opposite leaves are variable, often bearing broad teeth or shallow pointed lobes, and young stems are square in cross-section. Thickened underground roots help the plant persist. Native to southern Asia and grown for its flowers, it can become an environmental weed in warm regions such as Queensland. The blossoms attract bees, including large carpenter bees, and flowers may be followed by distinctly beaked capsules.

sources.label: Blue thunbergia — Brisbane City Council
Thunbergia grandiflora — Flora & Fauna Web

anguina-agrostis.summary: Bent-grass nematode is a microscopic roundworm that develops inside abnormal growths in grass flower heads. These elongated galls replace developing seeds and can be concealed by the surrounding flower parts. Bentgrasses are the best-known hosts, and a modern study also confirmed the species in fowl bluegrass beside a Wyoming river. Older accounts assigned many other grasses to this nematode, but some of those records belong to different species. Accurate identification therefore depends on examining the nematodes, not just noticing damaged seed heads.

sources.label: First report of Anguina agrostis from Poa palustris in Wyoming
First Report of Bentgrass Seed Gall Nematode in Virginia and Minnesota
Anguina agrostis — Nemaplex

agrostis-castellana.summary: Agrostis castellana is a perennial bentgrass with fine, gray-green leaves and upright flowering stems. It forms tufts linked by slender underground stems, while its flower head spreads into a delicate branching shape and often narrows as it ages. The tiny flower clusters may be greenish or purple, with some bearing slender awns and others lacking them. Native around the Mediterranean and nearby Atlantic islands, it has been introduced elsewhere, including New Zealand, where it is known as dryland browntop.

sources.label: Agrostis castellana — Flora of New Zealand
Agrostis castellana — Plants of the World Online

lachnagrostis-filiformis.summary: Lachnagrostis filiformis is a fine-leaved grass native to Australia, often growing on poorly drained or seasonally wet ground. Its loose, airy flower head branches widely above a tuft of narrow leaves, and the small green or purplish flower clusters carry bent bristles. At maturity, the stem commonly breaks beneath the flower head, allowing it to move away from the parent plant. Plants may behave as annuals or persist longer, and closely related grasses can be difficult to separate.

sources.label: Lachnagrostis filiformis — VicFlora
Lachnagrostis filiformis — Florabase

oxalis-pes-caprae.summary: Bermuda buttercup is a bulb-forming perennial from southern Africa, with bright yellow flowers held above a loose cluster of leaves. Each leaf has three heart-shaped leaflets, often dotted with purple. Despite its common name, it is a wood sorrel rather than a true buttercup. In California it grows during the cooler, wetter part of the year and retreats to underground bulbs as weather warms. Those bulbs allow patches to return and can spread the plant when contaminated soil is moved.

sources.label: Creeping Woodsorrel and Bermuda Buttercup
Oxalis pes-caprae — Flora of Iraq and Kew

cynodon-dactylon.summary: Bermudagrass is a low, wiry perennial grass that grows most actively in warm weather. It spreads through runners above ground and underground stems, both able to root and form new plants. Narrow leaves and fingerlike branches radiating from the tip of each flower stalk help distinguish a flowering patch. It is widely grown as turf, yet the same spreading growth makes it a persistent weed in gardens and planting beds. In cooler conditions the foliage turns brown as the grass becomes dormant.

sources.label: Bermudagrass — UC IPM
Bermudagrass — Utah State University

pinus-wallichiana.summary: Bhutan pine is an evergreen mountain tree from the Himalayan region, also known as Himalayan pine. Its long, gray-green needles grow in bundles of five and hang downward on older shoots, giving the branches a soft, drooping appearance. Long, resinous cones hang from stalks, while bark changes from smooth gray-green on young wood to darker, fissured scales with age. The species is grown as an ornamental beyond its native range and generally favors sunny sites with well-drained soil.

sources.label: Pinus wallichiana — Landscape Plants
Pinus wallichiana — Plants of the World Online

monomorium-floricola.summary: Bicolored trailing ants are tiny, shiny ants with a dark head and abdomen contrasting with a much lighter middle section. Workers are less than two millimeters long and often forage on trees, shrubs and around buildings in warm climates. Colonies occupy small cavities, including spaces in twigs and bark, and may contain several queens. The ants take insects and sweet foods, including honeydew from plant-feeding bugs. Their small nests can travel with nursery plants and other material moved by people.

sources.label: Monomorium floricola — Ants of Costa Rica
Two New Exotic Pest Ants Collected in Mississippi

cerastium-fontanum-ssp-vulgare.summary: Mouse-ear chickweed is a low, spreading perennial with small paired leaves and white flowers. Its softly hairy growth can blend into lawns until the flowers appear, each with five notched petals. Originally from Europe, it now grows widely in North America in fields, roadsides and other open, disturbed places. The flowers are small, with petals about as long as the green sepals beneath them. Those details help separate it from similar chickweeds.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust: Mouse-ear chickweed
Info Flora: Cerastium fontanum subsp. vulgare

briza-maxima.summary: Large quaking grass has flower clusters that hang like little paper lanterns from fine stalks. The overlapping scales can turn brown or purple, and the loose clusters give this annual grass its distinctive nodding look. Native to the Mediterranean region, it grows in disturbed ground and has become established beyond its original range. Narrow, flat leaves form loose tufts beneath the flower stems. Its conspicuous clusters make it easier to recognize than many grasses.

sources.label: PlantNET: Briza maxima
Flora of New Zealand: Briza maxima

lotus-uliginosus.summary: Big trefoil is a perennial member of the pea family, with yellow flowers gathered in clusters above its leaves. Each leaf has five leaflets, though the lower pair sits close to the stem and can be easy to overlook. Hollow stems and creeping shoots help distinguish its growth. Native to Eurasia and North Africa, it has become established elsewhere, including moist disturbed ground in southwestern British Columbia. You may also find it listed as Lotus pedunculatus.

sources.label: E-Flora BC: Lotus uliginosus
Flora of New Zealand: Lotus pedunculatus

hypophthalmichthys-nobilis.summary: Bighead carp are large freshwater fish with oversized heads, low-set eyes and irregular dark blotches along their bodies. Rather than hunting larger prey, they strain tiny organisms and other food from the water. Introduced from Asia for pond management, they escaped into rivers and now occur in parts of the Mississippi River system. Their appetite for plankton can put them in competition with native fish, including paddlefish and young fish that depend on the same food.

sources.label: Missouri Department of Conservation: Bighead carp
California Department of Fish and Wildlife: Bighead carp

centaurea-macrocephala.summary: Bighead knapweed is a sturdy perennial topped with large, bright yellow flower heads. Beneath each head, overlapping brown, papery scales form a rounded cup. Once grown as a garden ornamental, it has escaped cultivation in parts of Washington, where it can compete with grasses. Its rough, pointed leaves become smaller farther up the stems. The showy flowers are followed by seeds that help it spread, making an escaped patch worth identifying before those heads mature.

sources.label: Stevens County: Bighead knapweed
Burke Herbarium: Centaurea macrocephala

pheidole-megacephala.summary: Bigheaded ants get their name from the unusually large heads of their larger workers, which forage alongside many smaller ants. These small brown ants nest in soil, lawns and sheltered spaces beneath paving or pots, often leaving loose piles of sand. They feed on insects and sweet liquids such as honeydew. Established in many warm regions, including Florida, their large colonies can displace other ants and become a persistent household nuisance. Related native ants make careful identification important.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: Bigheaded ant
Western Australia DPIRD: Coastal brown ants

setaria-megaphylla.summary: Broadleaf bristlegrass is a tall, clump-forming perennial whose broad, pleated leaves can look quite different from ordinary lawn grasses. Its flowering stems carry long, branching clusters with fine bristles beside the small spikelets. It favors moist, sheltered places, including forest edges and stream margins, and has become established in Florida. Large rootstocks help the plant persist between growing seasons. A close look at the leaves and flower clusters is useful when separating it from other broad-leaved grasses.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Setaria megaphylla
SANBI PlantZAfrica: Setaria megaphylla

vinca-major.summary: Bigleaf periwinkle is an evergreen groundcover with trailing stems, broad paired leaves and blue-violet flowers. Planted in gardens for its dense cover, it can spread beyond beds when stems take root wherever they touch moist ground. Broken pieces can also travel in dumped garden waste or flowing water. Along shaded creeks and woodland edges in places such as California, established patches can crowd out native plants. Its larger, often heart-based leaves help distinguish it from small periwinkle.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Vinca major
California Invasive Plant Council: Vinca major

fenusa-pumila.summary: Birch leafminer is a small sawfly whose young feed between the upper and lower surfaces of birch leaves. Their feeding creates pale blotches that later turn brown, sometimes making a tree look badly scorched. Adults resemble tiny dark flies rather than wasps. Introduced to North America from the Old World, this species is one of several insects that mine birch leaves. Healthy, established trees often tolerate the damage, so brown foliage alone does not mean a tree is dying.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension: Birch leafminers
Kirichenko et al.: Global invasive leafminers

vicia-cracca.summary: Bird vetch is a climbing perennial with rows of small leaflets, curling tendrils and clusters of purple flowers gathered along one side of a stalk. It grows through meadows, roadsides and other open or disturbed places, using neighboring plants for support. Underground stems and seeds both help it spread. In Alaska, researchers have observed dense growth overtopping herbs and climbing shrubs at forest edges. Those tangled patches can change the space available to the vegetation beneath them.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust: Vicia cracca
University of Alaska Anchorage: Bird vetch risk assessment

lotus-corniculatus.summary: Birdsfoot trefoil is a low perennial with clusters of yellow pea-shaped flowers and slender seedpods that spread out like a bird's toes. Introduced as forage and for erosion control, it now grows along roadsides and in open grasslands. Its branching stems may lie close to the ground or rise above surrounding vegetation. In Minnesota and some other areas, it can crowd native prairie plants. Seeds can remain in the soil for years, allowing patches to return after the visible plants are removed.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension: Birdsfoot trefoil
Flora of New Zealand: Lotus corniculatus

sagina-procumbens.summary: Spreading pearlwort is a tiny perennial that forms low patches of slender stems and narrow leaves. It often grows in moist ground, lawns and cracks in paving, where its size makes it easy to overlook. The flowers are very small, with white petals that may be shorter than the surrounding green sepals or absent altogether. Some stems root where they touch the ground. This plant is native in parts of North America but introduced elsewhere, so its local status matters when interpreting a record.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust: Sagina procumbens
Flora of New Zealand: Sagina procumbens

veronica-persica.summary: Persian speedwell is a small annual with trailing, hairy stems and bright blue flowers marked with darker lines and a pale center. It often appears in gardens, crop fields, lawns and disturbed ground, flowering close to the soil surface. The rounded leaves have toothed edges, while individual flowers sit on thin stalks. It reproduces by seed and can grow through cool weather where conditions allow. Although easy to miss among larger weeds, a close look at the flowers usually reveals its distinctive pattern.

sources.label: UC IPM: Persian speedwell
Native Plant Trust: Veronica persica

aegopodium-podagraria.summary: Goutweed is a spreading perennial often planted as a leafy groundcover, including forms with creamy white leaf edges. Beneath the surface, branching rhizomes help it form dense patches that can be difficult to contain. Its leaves are divided into toothed leaflets, and small white flowers gather in broad, flat clusters above them. Originally from Europe and Asia, it has escaped gardens into shaded edges and woodlands. Dense growth can displace native herbs and leave less room for young trees to establish.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Ground elder
Wisconsin DNR: Bishop's goutweed

zingiber-zerumbet.summary: Shampoo ginger is a tropical perennial with upright leafy stems and cone-shaped flower heads on separate, shorter stalks. The overlapping bracts begin green and become red as they mature, with small pale flowers emerging between them. It spreads from creeping rhizomes and favors moist, sheltered places. Known as awapuhi in Hawai‘i, it was brought there by early Polynesian voyagers and has a long cultural history. Its leafy growth can die back seasonally, while the underground stems remain ready to grow again.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Zingiber zerumbet
National Tropical Botanical Garden: Zingiber zerumbet

cichlasoma-bimaculatum.summary: Black acara is a small, deep-bodied freshwater fish with two dark blotches, one near the middle of its side and another near the tail. Native to northern South America, it has become established in southern Florida, especially in shallow ditches and other disturbed waters. It eats a mixture of small animals and plant material, and both parents guard their young. Similar-looking chanchita have sometimes been mistaken for this species, so color and body shape alone are not enough for a confident identification.

sources.label: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Black acara
Robins et al.: Identification of acara established in Florida

phyllostachys-nigra.summary: Black bamboo is a tall evergreen grass best known for canes that emerge green and darken as they mature. Narrow leaves form light, arching sprays above the distinctive stems. Native to China, it is widely grown as an ornamental screen or garden feature. Although a planting may initially stay in a tight clump, underground rhizomes can send shoots farther out, particularly in warm, moist conditions. That spreading habit matters more for containment than the color of the canes.

sources.label: Royal Horticultural Society: Phyllostachys nigra
Trees and Shrubs Online: Phyllostachys nigra

brachyplatys-subaeneus.summary: Black bean bug is a small, shiny black insect that often gathers with others on plant stems and leaf stalks. Despite its beetle-like appearance, it is a true bug that feeds by sucking plant fluids. Pale yellow markings on its head and shoulders help distinguish it from other dark insects. Native to Asia and confirmed in southern Florida, it is associated particularly with legumes, including crop plants. Finding it on a plant does not necessarily mean it can complete its life cycle there.

sources.label: Florida Department of Agriculture: Black bean bug pest alert
Añino et al.: Black bean bug in Ecuador and host plants

fallopia-convolvulus.summary: Black bindweed, also called wild buckwheat, is an annual vine with pointed, arrow-shaped leaves and slender stems that trail or climb through nearby plants. Its tiny greenish flowers are easy to miss, especially beside the showier flowers of field bindweed, a different species. Introduced from Eurasia, it grows in crop fields, gardens, roadsides and other disturbed ground. It reproduces by seed, producing small, dark, three-sided fruits, and can become a troublesome tangle among crops.

sources.label: UC IPM: Wild buckwheat
Native Plant Trust: Fallopia convolvulus

mylopharyngodon-piceus.summary: Black carp is a large, dark fish with broad scales and powerful teeth deep in its throat that can crush snails and mussels. Brought from Asia for use in fish farming, it escaped into waterways and now reproduces in the Mississippi River basin. Its appetite raises concern for native freshwater mollusks, many of which already face other threats. Young black carp closely resemble grass carp, making careful identification important when unfamiliar fish are caught or moved.

sources.label: Missouri Department of Conservation: Black carp
USGS: Black carp biology, assessment and control
